short: Training tanks in unhardened steel, sent into battle at Arras for want of anything better.
full:
Fifty Mark IIs, twenty-five male and twenty-five female, were built by Foster's and Metropolitan between December 1916 and January 1917 as a stopgap while the Mark IV was designed. They were near-identical to the Mark I apart from a wider commander's hatch, a revised roof and the deletion of the wheeled steering tail, which had proved almost useless in mud. They were meant for driver training in Britain, and were built of unhardened plate that would not stop a rifle bullet.

When the Mark IV was not ready for the Arras offensive, the training machines were shipped to France, where about sixty Mark Is and Mark IIs went forward from 9 April 1917. The Germans had by then issued the K bullet, an armour-piercing rifle round, and it went through Mark II plate; several tanks were shot to pieces on the Arras battlefield. Survivors were turned into supply carriers, wireless tanks and gun-crew trainers. The Mark IV that followed carried hardened armour specified to defeat the same round.
